title: MB8-16399
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): Grounds for the Appeal The Minister appeals the decision for the following reasons:2 i) The Minister filed social media screenshots from the Respondent, her former husband (the agent of persecution), her current partner, and her children.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: I allow this appeal. The Appellant is the Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship (the Minister), and the respondent, XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of Hungary. Summary of Basis of Claim (BOC) narrative

The Respondent's father, chair of the local Roma Minority Organization, was found murdered on July 1, 2000. The respondent then joined this organization in September 2000. She was kidnapped and raped by three men on May 6, 2003, who spoke about her father's political activities. The Respondent was then forced to work as a XXXX XXXX, and then was sold to a man in Austria with whom she had three children. He became verbally and physically abusive when he learned the Respondent was Roma. With the help of her neighbour, she and the children escaped to Sweden in XXXX 2016, but fled to Germany in XXXX 2016, after her husband located them. Her husband found them again on March 10, 2017, and beat her up. She was able to escape with two of the children and return to Hungary in order to obtain passports which permitted them to come to Canada. Summary of the Refugee Protection Division Reasons for Decision

The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) allowed the Respondent's claim, but rejected those of her two children. It cited the following reasons to support its decision:1 i) The Respondent established a well-founded fear of persecution and is a Convention refugee; ii) The Respondent provided credible testimony and specific evidence to corroborate the incident of domestic abuse on July 23, 2014; iii) The Respondent's spouse is willing and able to pursue her to Hungary and, given the lack of state protection, she would continue to face sustained and systemic mistreatment upon her return to Hungary; iv) The Respondent does not have an internal flight alternative as a Roma in Hungary; and v) The Respondent's children are not Convention refugees because they are Austrian citizens who have adequate state protection in their country of citizenship. Grounds for the Appeal

The Minister appeals the decision for the following reasons:2 i) The Minister filed social media screenshots from the Respondent, her former husband (the agent of persecution), her current partner, and her children. New evidence obtained by the Minister negatively affects the Respondent's credibility; ii) The Respondent did not disclose that she had a passport and travelled to London, United Kingdom, on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017; iii) The Respondent did not disclose that she was in a relationship with her current partner in October 2016, before coming to Canada; iv) The Respondent was in contact with her husband and daughter on social media while she was seeking refugee protection from him. Summary of Refugee Protection Division (RAD) Reasons for Decision

The determinative issues for the appeal are credibility and lack of subjective fear of persecution. The Minister filed evidence which shows that the Respondent was in London, England, in February 2017 when she claimed to have been in Germany without a passport. The Respondent did not tell the truth about her passports and international travel at a material time. She also returned voluntarily to Hungary in XXXX 2020, and asked that her refugee protection be revoked.3 Given her significant misrepresentation before the RPD, the presumption of truth has been rebutted. In addition, her re-availment is indicative of a lack of subjective fear.

The appeal is allowed. I substitute my own decision that the Respondent is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.4 NEW EVIDENCE The evidence presented by the Appellant is accepted

The restriction on new evidence found in subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) only applies to the person who is the subject of the appeal (the Respondent), and not to the Minister. Nevertheless, the Respondent has a right to file responding documents. She did not do so. The documents filed by the Minister are admissible.
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.5

The Respondent filed one document in support of her claim. An Austrian police report dated July 23, 2014 states that the police were called to a youth gathering at a neighbouring house at which the Respondent and her children were present.6 Her husband was verbally abusive, but did not become violent. Reference is made to the use of a substance as being a contributing factor. Although she stated in her BOC narrative that she was beaten on July 23, 2014, the police report contradicts this. The RPD failed to note this. No police report was provided which indicates that her husband was ever physically violent, notwithstanding her allegation that she was beaten daily. The RPD did not provide adequate reasons to account for the evidentiary problems.

The Respondent testified that she fled to Sweden with the children in XXXX 2016, but was found by her husband in December. She then went to Germany, but her husband was able to find her on March 10, 2017 and beat her. She returned to Hungary and made an urgent application for a passport. After receiving it, she took the first available flight to Canada.

The Minister filed a Facebook screenshot which shows that the Respondent was in London, United Kingdom, on February 25, 2017.7 This evidence establishes that, more likely than not, the Respondent was not in Germany without a passport at that time, as alleged. The passport disclosed by the Respondent was issued on March 13, 2017, four days before her trip to Canada.8 She likely had a previous passport which she used for international travel which was not disclosed. The Respondent likely failed to tell the truth concerning her whereabouts in February 2017, her possession of a passport, and about her international travel. This constitutes a material misrepresentation of important facts which prevented the RPD from properly assessing the claim.

The Respondent has two daughters, one of whom lives with her and the other, XXXX XXXX XXXX.9, is with her husband in Austria. The Minister filed Facebook screenshots for the Respondent, her current partner, her husband, and her daughters. However, the Minister did not provide English or French translations of the posts which are either in German or Hungarian. In addition, the Minister did not refer to specific pages or make submissions about their significance. The mere fact that the Respondent may have had some contact with her daughter in Austria does not undermine her claim. I give this disclosure no probative value.

The Respondent filed a Notice of Withdrawal of an Appeal on November 4, 2010, because she was planning to return to Hungary with her two children.10 Given that she is not the Appellant, she has no authority to withdraw the appeal. She also stated that she is no longer represented by counsel.11

The Minister filed a Memorandum with additional evidence on December 1, 2020. A statement from the Respondent was filed which indicates that she wants to withdraw her refugee protection and voluntarily leave Canada.12 A flight schedule shows that the Respondent is returning to Hungary on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020.13

The Respondent executed a Statutory Declaration on November 9, 2020, which states that she is voluntarily returning to Hungary. She confirms that the Minister may use the Declaration to have her refugee protection revoked, and she does not oppose this. She renounces her right to an oral hearing before the RAD, and she consents to the appeal being decided in her absence.14 Screenshots of the Respondent's social media with her current partner were also filed.15

The Respondent obtained refugee protection based on testimony, which was not true, and then voluntarily returned to Hungary. The RPD accepted the risk based on a police report, which contradicted her testimony, but failed to account for this in its reasons for decision. Although the Respondent testified that she was beaten on many occasions, the RPD did not ask her why she did not provide any police reports about this. In light of mistakes made at the hearing, and new evidence which establishes material misrepresentation and re-availment, I am satisfied that the Minister has established that the Respondent lacks a subjective fear of persecution and that she is not at real risk in accordance with section 97 of the IRPA. The Respondent does not have a well-founded fear of persecution in Hungary, nor is she at risk of likely being killed, tortured, or subject to cruel or unusual treatment or punishment.

The appeal is allowed. Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(b) of the IRPA, I substitute my own decision that the Respondent is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. (signed) H.
